verse.text: What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we looked at and our hands touched, concerning the Logos of life—

note.traditional: That which was from the beginning

verse.note: The opening pronouns are neuter (“what,” not “who”), so the subject is not simply a person but everything the witnesses heard, saw and touched. “The beginning” may mean the absolute beginning, as in John 1:1, or the beginning of Jesus’ ministry and of the proclamation about him. Interpreters are divided, and the echo of the Gospel’s opening may be deliberate in either case.

Nearly all translations use “Word.” This translation keeps the Greek term as a title, as in John 1:1, because “the Word” now commonly suggests the Bible. To a Greek-speaking reader the term also suggested reason and the order of the world, though most scholars see its main background in the Hebrew Bible’s “word of the Lord” and Wisdom traditions, which “Word” reflects better. Here specifically, many interpreters think the phrase means “the message about life” rather than the personal Word, since verse 2 goes on to speak of “the life,” not “the Word”; the question is open.

verse.text: and the life was revealed, and we have seen it and testify and announce to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us—
verse.note: In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, a matter of kind as well as length. Here it is spoken of as something that “was with the Father” and then appeared, language very close to what John 1:1–2 says of the Logos.

verse.text: what we have seen and heard we announce to you also, so that you too may have fellowship with us. And indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.
And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.

note.traditional: your joy (KJV); our joy (most modern versions)

verse.note: Manuscripts are divided in two places in this verse: some read “we write these things to you” where the text has an emphatic “we are writing,” and some read “your joy” for “our joy.” The Greek words for “our” and “your” differ by one letter and were pronounced alike, so confusion was easy. Most editors prefer “our joy” as the reading that copyists were more likely to change.

verse.text: And this is the message that we have heard from him and declare to you: that God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all.
If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in the darkness, we lie and do not do the truth.
verse.note: The Greek says literally “do the truth,” a Semitic turn of phrase also found in John 3:21 and in Jewish writings of the period, where truth is something acted out and not only spoken. Most modern versions smooth it to “practice the truth” or “live by the truth.” The literal form is kept here because it balances “we lie” and shows that the author treats truth as a matter of conduct.

verse.text: But if we walk in the light as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.
If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
verse.note: Most English versions read “faithful and just.” Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice), and the “unrighteousness” at the end of the verse is the negative of the same word. “Righteous” keeps that link visible: the one who is in the right removes what is not right. The sense is not that God is strict in punishing, but that he acts rightly and reliably in forgiving.

verse.text: If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
verse.note: The Greek noun is the same one rendered “Logos” in verse 1, but here it has its ordinary sense of God’s spoken message, parallel to “the truth is not in us” in verse 8. The title is therefore not used. A reader of the Greek would notice the repetition, which English cannot show without confusing the two senses.

verse.text: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you will not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, the righteous one,
and he himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the whole world.
verse.note: The noun occurs in the New Testament only here and at 4:10. “Propitiation” (turning away wrath) is the older English rendering, and some prefer “expiation” (removing sin); which nuance is uppermost is a long-running dispute. “Atoning sacrifice” keeps the sacrificial associations the word family has in the Greek Old Testament without deciding that question, and several modern versions use it.

verse.text: And by this we know that we have come to know him: if we keep his commandments.
Whoever says, “I have come to know him,” and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in that person;
but whoever keeps his word—in that person the love of God has truly been perfected. By this we know that we are in him:
verse.note: The Greek can mean a person’s love for God, God’s love for that person, or the kind of love that comes from God, and interpreters are divided. The English phrase is left as open as the Greek. “Perfected” here means brought to its goal or full expression, not made flawless.

verse.text: whoever says, “I remain in him,” ought also to walk just as he walked.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for staying or continuing somewhere, and it runs through this chapter (verses 6, 10, 14, 17, 19, 24, 27, 28). “Abide” is the traditional rendering and is still used by several versions, but it is archaic in everyday English and hides the link with plain uses such as “they would have remained with us” in verse 19. “Remain” is used throughout so the repetition can be heard.

verse.text: Beloved, I am not writing you a new commandment but an old commandment, which you have had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you heard.
And yet it is a new commandment I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.
Whoever says, “I am in the light,” and hates their brother or sister is still in the darkness.
verse.note: The Greek is grammatically masculine singular, but the word was the community’s ordinary term for a fellow member, whether a man or a woman. Many translations keep “his brother”; others, as here, spell out the inclusive sense and use singular “their” for the person concerned.

verse.text: Whoever loves their brother or sister remains in the light, and in that person there is no cause for stumbling.

note.term: in that person there is no cause for stumbling
note.traditional: there is no occasion of stumbling in him

verse.note: The noun means a trap or obstacle that makes someone fall. The Greek pronoun can refer to the person who loves (nothing in them trips up themselves or others) or to the light (“in it there is nothing to stumble over”), which would suit the picture of walking blind in verse 11. Most translations take it of the person, as here.

verse.text: But whoever hates their brother or sister is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where they are going, because the darkness has blinded their eyes.
I am writing to you, little children, because your sins have been forgiven on account of his name.
verse.note: Six times in verses 12–14 the Greek conjunction can mean either “because” (giving the reason for writing) or “that” (giving the content of what is written). Most translations choose “because”, as here. The shift from “I am writing” to “I have written” is usually thought to be stylistic, though its significance is debated.

verse.text: I am writing to you, fathers, because you have come to know the one who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have conquered the evil one.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for winning a battle, a contest or a court case. “Overcome” is the traditional rendering and remains common, but in modern English it can suggest merely getting past a difficulty. “Conquer” keeps the note of victory; the meaning itself is not in dispute.

verse.text: I have written to you, children, because you have come to know the Father. I have written to you, fathers, because you have come to know the one who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you, and you have conquered the evil one.
Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in that person,
because everything in the world—the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes and the pride in possessions—is not from the Father but is from the world.
verse.note: The first noun means boastful pretension, and the second is not the usual word for life but one meaning livelihood or material means; at 3:17 the same word means worldly goods. The traditional “pride of life” is kept by several versions, while others have “pride in riches” or “pride in one’s lifestyle”. The phrase describes showing off what one has.

verse.text: And the world is passing away, along with its desire, but whoever does the will of God remains forever.
Children, it is the last hour, and just as you heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have arisen. From this we know that it is the last hour.
verse.note: In the New Testament the word occurs only in 1 and 2 John. It means one who opposes the Christ, and possibly one who puts himself in the Christ’s place. The readers had been taught to expect such a figure before the end; the author applies the term to people who have left the community and deny that Jesus is the Christ (verses 19 and 22).

verse.text: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us. But they went out so that it might be revealed that none of them is of us.
But you have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know.
verse.note: The Greek word shares its root with “Christ” (the anointed one) and “antichrist”, a play on words a Greek reader would have heard: those who belong to the Anointed have themselves been anointed. Most interpreters take the anointing to be the Holy Spirit; some take it to be the teaching received at the beginning. “The Holy One” may be God or Jesus.

Many manuscripts read “you know all things”, differing by one short word ending, and older English versions follow them. The reading translated here is the one printed in the SBLGNT and most modern editions. It fits the argument that knowledge of the truth belongs to the whole community and not to a select few.

verse.text: I have not written to you because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is from the truth.
Who is the liar, if not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist: the one who denies the Father and the Son.
No one who denies the Son has the Father either; whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well.
As for you, let what you heard from the beginning remain in you. If what you heard from the beginning remains in you, you too will remain in the Son and in the Father.
And this is the promise that he himself made to us: eternal life.
I have written these things to you about those who are trying to lead you astray.

As for you, the anointing that you received from him remains in you, and you have no need for anyone to teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about all things, and is true and is no lie, and just as it has taught you, remain in him.
verse.note: The Greek verb form can be a command (“remain”) or a statement (“you remain”), and the pronoun can mean “in him” or “in it”, that is, in the anointing or its teaching. The unambiguous command “remain in him” at the start of verse 28 supports the reading chosen here, but translations differ.

verse.text: And now, little children, remain in him, so that when he is revealed we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.
If you know that he is righteous, you also know that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
See what kind of love the Father has given us: that we should be called children of God—and we are. The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know him.
verse.note: These words are present in the earliest manuscripts but missing from most later ones, which is why the King James Version does not have them. They are generally accepted as original.

verse.text: Beloved, we are children of God now, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that when he is revealed we will be like him, because we will see him as he is.
verse.note: The Greek verb has no stated subject, so the clause can also be read “when it is revealed,” meaning what we will be. “He” is chosen because the same phrase in 2:28 refers to Christ’s coming and the next words speak of seeing him. Both readings have scholarly support.

verse.text: And everyone who has this hope in him purifies themselves, just as he is pure.
verse.note: Here and in verses 5, 7 and 16 the Greek uses an emphatic pronoun, literally “that one.” In this letter it regularly points to Jesus. The plain “him” elsewhere in the chapter is often ambiguous between God and Christ, and the translation leaves that ambiguity in place.

verse.text: Everyone who practices sin also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.
And you know that he was revealed to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.
No one who remains in him sins; no one who sins has seen him or known him.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for staying or continuing somewhere. “Abide” is traditional in John’s writings but is no longer everyday English. “Remain” is used throughout the chapter so that the repetition stays visible.

note.term: No one who remains in him sins

verse.note: The Greek present tense can describe a continuing pattern, so many versions render “keeps on sinning” here and in verse 9, which eases the tension with 1:8–2:1, where the author says that claiming to be without sin is self-deception. Whether the tense alone carries that weight is disputed. The translation leaves the statement as stark as the Greek and does not resolve the question.

verse.text: Little children, let no one deceive you. The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous.
The one who practices sin is from the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The Son of God was revealed for this purpose: to undo the works of the devil.
verse.note: The verb’s basic use is loosening or untying, and by extension dismantling, annulling or bringing something to an end. “Destroy” is the usual rendering and is not wrong. “Undo” keeps the sense of reversing what the devil has done.

verse.text: No one who has been born of God practices sin, because his seed remains in them; and they cannot sin, because they have been born of God.
verse.note: The image is most often taken as God’s own life-giving principle, variously identified as his word, his Spirit or the new nature, implanted in the believer as a father’s seed begets a child. Because the word can also mean “offspring,” a minority reads “God’s offspring remain in him,” that is, in God. The translation follows the majority reading.

verse.text: By this it is clear who are the children of God and who are the children of the devil: everyone who does not practice righteousness is not from God, and neither is the one who does not love their brother or sister.
verse.note: The Greek word, literally “brother,” was the ordinary term for a fellow member of the community regardless of sex, and its plural regularly included women. It is rendered “brother or sister” and “brothers and sisters” where a fellow believer is meant, and “brother” for Cain’s actual brother in verse 12. Several modern versions do the same.

verse.text: For this is the message you heard from the beginning: that we should love one another—
not like Cain, who was from the evil one and slaughtered his brother. And why did he slaughter him? Because his own works were evil and his brother’s were righteous.
verse.note: The verb is stronger than the usual words for killing. It was used for slaughtering animals, especially in sacrifice, and for butchering people violently. Elsewhere in the New Testament it occurs only in Revelation. Most modern versions soften it to “murdered,” which also blurs the distinction from the different word for “murderer” in verse 15.

verse.text: Do not be surprised, brothers and sisters, if the world hates you.
We know that we have crossed over from death into life, because we love our brothers and sisters. The one who does not love remains in death.
Everyone who hates their brother or sister is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in them.
By this we have come to know love: he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers and sisters.
But whoever has the world’s goods and sees their brother or sister in need, yet shuts off compassion from them—how does the love of God remain in such a person?
Little children, let us not love with word or with tongue, but in deed and in truth.
By this we will know that we are from the truth, and before him we will reassure our hearts

note.traditional: shall assure our hearts before him. For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart

verse.note: The grammar of verses 19–20 is among the most difficult in the letter. The verb can mean “persuade” or “set at rest,” and the connecting word that opens verse 20 can be read as “that,” “because” or “whenever.” The rendering follows the common view that God’s greater knowledge is a comfort to a self-accusing conscience. Some have instead taken it as a warning that God judges more strictly than the heart does.

verse.text: whenever our hearts condemn us; for God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything.
Beloved, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God,
verse.note: The word originally meant freedom to speak one’s mind, and by this period it also meant the assurance of someone who can stand before a superior without fear or shame. “Confidence” conveys this better than “boldness,” which can suggest audacity. Most modern versions make the same choice here, and the difference is one of English nuance more than of meaning.

verse.text: and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what is pleasing in his sight.
And this is his commandment: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he commanded us.
Whoever keeps his commandments remains in him, and he in them. And by this we know that he remains in us: by the Spirit he has given us.
Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world.
By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that acknowledges Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is from God,
verse.note: The verb means to declare openly or to affirm something as true. “Confess” is the traditional rendering, but in modern English it mainly suggests admitting guilt, which is not the sense here. Several modern translations also use “acknowledge.”

note.term: Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh
note.traditional: that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh

verse.note: The Greek can be construed in more than one way: “acknowledges Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh,” “acknowledges that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh,” or “acknowledges Jesus as the Christ who has come in the flesh.” All three make the same basic point, that the true confession is of a Jesus who was really human. Which nuance is intended is disputed.

verse.text: and every spirit that does not acknowledge Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming, and it is now already in the world.

note.traditional: confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh

verse.note: Many later manuscripts expand this to match verse 2 (“does not acknowledge that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh”), which is the reading behind the King James Version. A few ancient witnesses, mainly Latin, read “every spirit that annuls Jesus.” The shorter reading translated here has the best manuscript support.

verse.text: You are from God, little children, and you have conquered them, because the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for winning a victory in battle, in the games or in court. “Overcome,” the traditional rendering, now tends to suggest only getting past a difficulty; “conquer” keeps the note of victory and the link with the same verb in John 16:33 and Revelation. The meaning is not disputed, and some modern translations also use “conquer” here.

verse.text: They are from the world; that is why they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.
We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. From this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.
Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.
Whoever does not love has not come to know God, because God is love.
In this the love of God was revealed among us: God has sent his one and only Son into the world so that we might live through him.
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean “among us,” “in us” or “to us.” The same phrase is rendered “in us” in verse 12 and “for us” in verse 16, where the context points in those directions. Here the reference to a public event, the sending of the Son, favors “among us,” but “in us” is possible.

The word means “only one of its kind” and was the usual term for an only child. Its second element is related to “kind,” not to “beget,” so most modern translations have “only” or “one and only.” A minority of scholars have recently defended “only begotten.”

verse.text: In this is love: not that we have loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins.
verse.note: The traditional “propitiation” means the turning away of wrath; others prefer “expiation,” the removal of sin. The word belongs to the Greek Old Testament’s vocabulary of atonement, and which emphasis it carries here is a long-running dispute. “Atoning sacrifice” is used because it is intelligible to modern readers and leaves that question open.

verse.text: Beloved, if this is how God loved us, we also ought to love one another.
No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God remains in us and his love has been perfected in us.
verse.note: The verb is the everyday Greek word for staying or continuing somewhere, and it is a key term in this letter and in John’s Gospel. “Abide” is now archaic and can sound more mysterious than the Greek does. “Remain” is used throughout the chapter so that the repetition is visible.

The verb means to bring something to its goal or full state, and it is agreed that the idea is of love reaching its intended end and not of flawlessness. Some translations have “made complete.” “Perfected” is kept so that the link with “perfect love” in verse 18 is visible. “His love” may be God’s love for us, our love for God, or the kind of love that is God’s own.

verse.text: By this we know that we remain in him and he in us: he has given us a share of his Spirit.
And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent the Son as Savior of the world.
Whoever acknowledges that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in them and they in God.
And we have come to know and believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in them.
In this, love has been perfected with us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment; for just as he is, so also are we in this world.
verse.note: The word originally meant freedom to speak one’s mind, and by this period it also meant the assurance of someone who can stand before a superior without fear or shame. “Boldness,” the traditional rendering, can suggest nerve or audacity, which is not the point when facing judgment. Many modern translations also have “confidence” here; the difference is one of English nuance, not of meaning.

The Greek pronoun is literally “that one,” which this letter regularly uses to refer to Jesus (for example 2:6; 3:3, 5, 7, 16). The thought is that believers, while still in this world, already share Jesus’s standing with the Father, and so can face the day of judgment without fear.

verse.text: There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear, because fear has to do with punishment, and the one who fears has not been perfected in love.
We love because he first loved us.
verse.note: Many manuscripts add an object, either “him” (the reading behind the King James Version) or “God.” The shorter reading is better attested and is the one translated. The Greek verb form could also be read as an exhortation, “Let us love,” though most interpreters take it as a statement.

verse.text: If anyone says, “I love God,” and hates their brother or sister, that person is a liar; for whoever does not love their brother or sister, whom they have seen, cannot love God, whom they have not seen.
verse.note: The Greek has the masculine singular “his brother,” used generically for any fellow member of the believing community, man or woman. “Brother or sister,” with singular “their,” conveys that scope to a modern reader; several modern translations do the same, while others keep “brother.”

verse.text: And this is the commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love their brother or sister.
Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the father loves also the one born of him.
verse.note: The Greek uses one verb three times in this verse: “has been born,” “the one who fathered,” and “the one fathered by him.” The second clause can be read as a general maxim (whoever loves a father loves his child too) or as a direct statement about God and fellow believers. The lowercase “father” leaves both readings open; the application to God and his children follows in the next verse either way.

verse.text: By this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God and carry out his commandments.
For this is love for God: that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome,
because everything that has been born of God conquers the world. And this is the victory that has conquered the world: our faith.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for winning a battle or contest, and “victory” in the same verse is its cognate noun. “Overcome,” the rendering of the KJV and many modern versions, now tends to suggest merely getting past a difficulty; “conquer” keeps the note of victory and the link with John 16:33 and the promises to the victor in Revelation. The meaning itself is not disputed.

verse.text: Who is the one who conquers the world, if not the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?

This is the one who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ—not with the water only, but with the water and with the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.
verse.note: The author does not explain the phrase, and its meaning is debated. The most common view takes the water as Jesus’ baptism and the blood as his death, with the insistence on “not the water only” aimed at opponents who denied the significance of his death. Others see a reference to the water and blood that flowed from Jesus’ side (John 19:34), or to baptism and the Lord’s Supper.

verse.text: For there are three that testify:

note.traditional: For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness in earth

verse.note: The longer wording familiar from the KJV, naming the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit as three witnesses in heaven, is absent from all early Greek manuscripts and from the earliest translations. It arose in the Latin tradition and entered printed Greek editions in the sixteenth century. Scholars are virtually unanimous that it is not part of the original letter.

verse.text: the Spirit and the water and the blood, and the three are in agreement.
If we accept human testimony, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God: that he has testified about his Son.
Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony within. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because they have not believed in the testimony that God has given about his Son.
And this is the testimony: that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
verse.note: The adjective derives from the word for “age,” and in Jewish usage “eternal life” meant the life of the age to come—a matter of kind as well as of duration. “Eternal” is the standard rendering and is kept here; a minority of translators prefer “life of the age to come.” The author’s point is that this life is already given and possessed in the Son.

verse.text: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.
I have written these things to you so that you may know that you have eternal life—you who believe in the name of the Son of God.
And this is the confidence we have before him: that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us.
verse.note: The Greek word originally meant freedom to speak one’s mind and came to include the assurance of someone who can stand before a superior without fear or shame. It is often rendered “boldness” elsewhere, and some versions use that here; “confidence” is chosen because “boldness” can suggest nerve or audacity, which is not the point in approaching God in prayer. The difference is one of English nuance, not of meaning.

verse.text: And if we know that he hears us, whatever we ask, we know that we have what we have asked of him.

If anyone sees a brother or sister committing a sin that does not lead to death, they should ask, and God will give that person life—that is, to those whose sin does not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I am not saying that anyone should make a request about that.
verse.note: The Greek has the masculine singular “his brother,” which in this letter means any fellow member of the community, male or female. “Brother or sister” conveys what the first readers would have understood. Several modern versions do the same; others keep “brother.”

note.term: God will give that person life

verse.note: The Greek says only “he will ask, and he will give him life,” without naming the subject of “give.” Most interpreters take God as the giver, and the translation supplies “God” for clarity; grammatically the one who prays could be the subject, giving life by means of the prayer. The future “he will ask” functions as an instruction and is rendered “should ask.”

The author assumes his readers know what he means and does not define it. Proposals include deliberate, defiant sin as distinguished from unwitting sin in the Law; the rejection of Christ by those who had left the community (compare 2:19); and sin that results in physical death. No view commands agreement, and the author does not forbid prayer in such a case; he says only that he is not asking for it.

verse.text: All wrongdoing is sin, and there is sin that does not lead to death.
We know that no one who has been born of God sins; rather, the one who was born of God keeps them safe, and the evil one does not touch them.
verse.note: The Greek present tense can describe either a simple fact or a habitual practice. Some translations render “does not keep on sinning” to ease the tension with 1:8, where the author says that those who claim to have no sin deceive themselves. Whether the tense alone can bear that distinction is disputed, so the plain rendering is kept.

note.term: the one who was born of God keeps them safe
note.traditional: he that is begotten of God keepeth himself

verse.note: The Greek text followed here reads “keeps him,” and “the one who was born of God” is most naturally Jesus, the Son, who protects the believer. Many manuscripts read “keeps himself,” making the believer the one who is born of God and who guards himself; the KJV follows that reading. Most modern editions and translations prefer the reading adopted here, though the matter is not settled.

verse.text: We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.
And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true one; and we are in the true one, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.

note.term: He is the true God and eternal life
note.traditional: This is the true God, and eternal life

verse.note: The Greek pronoun “this one” could point to Jesus Christ, the nearest antecedent, or back to “the true one,” the Father, whom the Son has made known. Many interpreters take it of Jesus, noting that he is called “the eternal life” at the opening of the letter (1:2); others take it of the Father, since “the true one” has just been distinguished from “his Son.” The English “He” leaves the question open as the Greek does.

verse.text: Little children, guard yourselves from idols.
